title: Chennai Entrepreneur's Viral Post Reopens India's Work-Life Balance Debate
excerpt: Sundara Rajan says he worked up to 14-hour days, six-and-a-half days a week, at a construction firm from 1986 to 1994 — needing four hours' permission just for a haircut — reviving the 70-hour workweek debate sparked by Narayana Murthy and L&T's S. N. Subrahmanyan.
body:
• Chennai businessman Sundara Rajan says he routinely worked 10 to 14 hours a day, six-and-a-half days a week, during an eight-year stint at a private construction company from 1986 to 1994 — an account that has drawn more than 3 million views on X.
  • Rajan recalled needing up to four hours of formal permission during weekdays just to run personal errands like banking, posting mail, phoning home or getting a haircut.
  • Online reaction was split: some questioned presenting such schedules as normal construction work, while others said deadline-driven project work can genuinely demand long continuity from the same people.
  • Indian law caps factory work at 48 hours a week (60 with overtime) under the Factories Act, 1948, with one weekly rest day mandatory; the WHO recommends 35-40 hours a week. A 14-hour day, six-and-a-half days a week, is roughly 91 hours — well beyond both.

Opening news lead

A Chennai-based entrepreneur has reignited India's long-running work-life balance debate with a candid recollection of what he describes as a punishing work routine more than three decades ago. Sundara Rajan, posting on X, said that during his time at a private construction company between 1986 and 1994, site staff routinely worked between 10 and 14 hours a day, six-and-a-half days a week — and that even the most ordinary personal errands had to be squeezed into the workday with formal permission.

Context & Background

According to the coverage by LiveMint and TechWordNews, Rajan claimed project managers "would lead from the front" and that the demanding schedule was simply the working environment at project sites at the time. He said he would need up to four hours of permission during weekdays for errands such as banking, sending mail, phoning home and cutting hair — a detail that struck a chord with thousands of readers who recognised the shape of a life with no slack in it.

Rajan also pushed back on criticism, arguing that construction work comes in waves — periods of relative calm alongside crunch periods — and that thin margins and operational complexity in the sector make continuity from the same person important. He added that the US construction industry can involve similarly demanding schedules, though workers there are paid better. His account is personal and historical: it does not prove the same conditions persist in the industry today.

"I don't believe in work-life balance."

— N. R. Narayana Murthy, Infosys co-founder, at the CNBC TV18 Global Leadership Summit

Impact & Analysis

The post landed in a debate that has been simmering in India for two years. It began with Infosys co-founder Narayana Murthy's controversial suggestion that young Indians should work 70-hour weeks — a remark he later doubled down on, saying he himself worked 14-hour days, six-and-a-half days a week, for 30 years until retiring in 2011. L&T chairman S. N. Subrahmanyan then pushed the envelope further, floating a 90-hour workweek and wondering aloud why employees need weekends at all. ITC chairman Sanjiv Puri countered, arguing that empowering employees and flexible arrangements beat hour-counting.

The numbers in Rajan's account dwarf even the most extreme of those public prescriptions. A 14-hour day across six-and-a-half days totals about 91 hours a week — more than double India's legal factory ceiling and well above the global norm. Public-health research backs the sceptics: prolonged weeks of 55+ hours are associated with higher cardiovascular risk and burnout, and the economic case for endless hours typically ignores the hidden costs of errors, attrition and healthcare.

Diaspora Angle

The hustle-culture debate doesn't stop at India's borders. Indian professionals abroad — from H-1B workers in US tech to finance staff in London and Singapore — often carry the same work-until-you-drop expectations into workplaces where the norms differ sharply, and some quietly report that their Indian upbringing makes it harder to push back. Murthy's and Subrahmanyan's remarks travelled far in diaspora WhatsApp groups precisely because they touch that tension: pride in the work ethic versus the price paid in health and family time. For diaspora managers hiring or leading teams in India, Rajan's account is a useful reminder of how recently — and how recently normalised — extreme schedules were.

What's Next

India's workplace conversation shows no sign of settling. With attrition rising in white-collar sectors, India's largest IT firms experimenting with flexible models, and younger workers openly rating employers on culture, the 70-hour and 90-hour pronouncements of 2024-25 already look dated to many. Rajan's viral post adds a memoir to the argument — and leaves the open question he posed: how much of a person's week should any job be allowed to claim?
nri_angle: Indian professionals abroad navigate the same hustle-culture expectations — from H-1B tech workers to Gulf engineers — and the Murthy/Subrahmanyan remarks landed in diaspora circles because they capture the tension between pride in the work ethic and its cost in health and family time.
author: Diaspora Desk
